newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-IRISH DOWNHILLER BUCKS THE TREND.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-IRISH DOWNHILLER BUCKS THE TREND.

text.p: Ireland's small band of intrepid Alpine skiers traditionally learn their craft on artificial slopes before trying out real snow.
Paul Schwarzacher-Joyce, the first Irish downhiller for years, has done it the other way round.
Brought up in Austria with an Austrian father and Irish mother, as his double-barreled name rather suggests, he learned to ski on the natural stuff in the Alps.
He then moved on to dry slopes in Ireland.

"In September and October I was racing in the Irish championships on plastic," the 24-year-old student of ecology and sport from Salzburg said on Tuesday after the opening downhill training of the world championships.
"That was great fun. It was different."
At the 1993 Morioka championships in Japan, the Irish provided one of the better quotes when they insisted they were not overawed by the sport's big events.
"We've done all the big races. Hillend, Rosendale, Llandudno," said student Shane O'Connor then, referring to the artificial pistes within their reach.
Four years on the Irish have found someone who has not merely raced down real mountains before but one who has done the big one -- Kitzbuehel's dreaded Streif.

"I skied in Kitzbuehel as a forerunner and that was a great experience," said Schwarzacher-Joyce, who was brought up bilingual but whose parental Austrian accent comes out slightly ahead of his Dublin one.
"I just like the speed events."
Dry slope skiing hardly satisfied that lust for speed but the Irish Austrian, or Austrian Irishman, was not going to be sniffy about the conditions found in Dublin.

"It's short. Everybody has the same conditions. You don't need so much feeling for controlling all the bumps. But you have to be very good technically, your body has to be very exact. Actually, sometimes it's more difficult than on snow."
Schwarzacher-Joyce raced in Austria until he was about 16 or 17 before giving it up for the greater allure of snowboard racing, which he followed for a further five years.
Last year he returned to skiing, got a licence for Ireland and entered what is his first world championship.
"I'm trying my best with no training at all," he said. "On the continent I am the only one from Ireland so I am travelling around alone, doing it on my own budget."
He is still looking for a sponsor in Ireland.
"Money-wise people don't really like to give out money to a sport which doesn't really exist in Ireland," he said.
"I hope if I do well in these races and they know we have an Iirish downhiller, the interest may grow in skiing."
Irish team leader John Barrett said nobody else in Ireland, where there is a ''thriving plastic professional skiing" circuit, could boast of a season on snow like him.
For those who may consider him more of an Austrian in disguise, Schwarzacher-Joyce points out that he has spent a lot of time there and has many Irish relatives.
"When I am there I feel they accept me. They have a good sense of humour and don't take it so seriously.
"I feel Irish," he said. "I mean, my legs might be Austrian but my head is Irish."
